title: Is Spurious Correlation Removal Always Learnable?
claim: The best efficient algorithm needs far more samples than unrestricted search to reach the same accuracy, and the gap widens with scale.
layout: single line plot, two series, hatched gap region with double-headed arrow
description: A single line chart with a grid background. A blue line with circle markers, labeled Exhaustive search, stays almost flat near zero across ten x positions. A red line with square markers, labeled Best poly-time, rises from about 500 to about 9,000 on the y-axis, which runs from 0 to 8,000+. The legend sits in the top-left. The region between the two curves is filled with light gray diagonal hatching. A bold black double-headed vertical arrow labeled Gap marks the separation near the middle-right. Multiplier annotations (4×, 21×, 27×) sit at points along the curves and show the ratio growing. The widening red-versus-blue separation draws the eye first. The x-axis and axis labels are cropped out.
caption: Compute--sample gap on synthetic instances: exhaustive search needs far fewer samples than the best polynomial-time method to reach the same feature-selection accuracy.
abstract: Invariant learning can fail even when the invariant structure is statistically identifiable. We show a conditional computational barrier: under a black-box samplable supervised sparse recovery primitive motivated by average-case sparse-recovery reductions, there exist \emph{samplable} multi-environment instances with a one-dimensional predictive invariant subspace ($k=1$) that are learnable with polynomial samples by exhaustive search, while any polynomial-time constant-accuracy recovery algorithm would contradict the primitive. We further quantify environment diversity by a separation parameter $Î³$, which controls identifiability and the curvature of invariance objectives. Under sufficient diversity and local Gaussian regularity, the minimax risk is $\mathbb{E}[\dist(\hat{V},V_{\mathrm{inv}})^2]=Î(k(d-k)/(n|\mathcal{E}|))$, and under label-induced shifts a phase transition occurs at $n^*\propto k(d-k)/(|\mathcal{E}|Î³^2)$ with refined estimation error scaling proportional to $1/Î³^2$. Synthetic and real datasets illustrate the predicted gaps and transitions and motivate simple diversity diagnostics.
